source_text: Εἰ δέ τις ἑτέρῳ ἐπιβουλεύει, λέληθεν αὑτὸν ὡς ἑαυτῷ πρώτῳ καὶ μόνῳ ἔνεδρον ἐργάζεται. Ὁ δὲ καθαιρῶν ἄλλου ἀσφάλειαν, περιπεσεῖται ὄφεως δήγματι. Ἀλλὰ μὴ [ἴσ. μὴν] ὁ λίθους ἐξαιρούμενος, ὑποίσει πόνον οὐ μικρόν· ἀλλὰ καὶ σχίζων ξύλα, ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ οἰκείῳ ὅπλῳ τὸν κίνδυνον οἴσει. Ἐὰν δὲ συμβῇ τοῦ στελεοῦ τὸν πέλεκυν ἐκπηδῆσαι, θορυβηθήσεται ὁ ταῦτα ἐργαζόμενος, οὐκ ἐπ᾽ ἀγαθῷ συγκομίζων, καὶ ἐπαύξων αὐτὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἄδικον καὶ ὠκύμορον δύναμιν. Ὄφεως δὲ δῆγμα λαθραῖον· οὐδὲν παραμυθήσονται οἱ ἐπᾴδοντες· μάταιοι γάρ εἰσιν. Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ μὲν ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὰ ἐργάζεται αὑτῷ τε καὶ τοῖς πλησίον· ὁ δὲ ἄφρων εἰς ὄλεθρον ἐμπεσεῖται διὰ τῆς αὐτοῦ φλυαρίας. Καὶ ἄπαξ ἀνοίξας τὸ στόμα, ἄρχεται ἀφρόνως, καὶ παύεται ταχέως, διὰ παντὸς ἐνδεικνύμενος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἄνοιαν.
thought_title: The plotter harms himself; the fool's chatter
orientation: The plotter harms himself first, and the fool ruins himself by his own chatter.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone plots against another, it has escaped his notice that he works an ambush for himself first and alone. The one pulling down another's safety will fall into a bite of a snake. But indeed the one extracting/quarrying stones will undergo not small toil; but also the one splitting wood will bear the danger in his very own tool/weapon. If it happens that the axe leaps off the handle, the one working these things will be troubled, not gathering for good, and himself increasing his own unjust and swift-fated power. A bite of a snake is secret; the charmers will console nothing; for they are vain. But the good man works good things for himself and for his neighbors; the fool will fall into destruction through his own babbling. And once having opened the mouth, he begins foolishly, and ceases quickly, through everything displaying his own senselessness.

pass_b_english: If anyone plots against another, he fails to see that he is laying an ambush first and only for himself (Ecclesiastes 10:8). The man who tears down another's security will fall prey to a serpent's bite (Ecclesiastes 10:8). Moreover, the man who quarries stones will bear no small toil, and the man who splits wood also carries danger in his very own tool (Ecclesiastes 10:9). If the axe happens to leap from its handle, the man at this work will be thrown into confusion (Ecclesiastes 10:10); he gathers to no good end, and he himself increases his own unjust and short-lived power.

A serpent's bite comes unseen; the charmers will bring no comfort, for they are useless (Ecclesiastes 10:11). But the good man does good both to himself and to his neighbors, while the fool will fall into ruin through his own chatter (Ecclesiastes 10:12). Once he opens his mouth, he begins foolishly and soon stops, showing his own senselessness at every turn (Ecclesiastes 10:13–14).
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:8-14. Doubtful reading: MGR prints 'Ἀλλὰ μὴ [ἴσ. μὴν]'; read ἀλλὰ μήν with the editor's bracket and the 1622 Latin 'Quin is etiam', rendered 'Moreover'. 'He gathers to no good end, and he himself only increases his own unjust and short-lived power' follows Gregory's turn on the LXX of Ecclesiastes 10:10 ('he will strengthen his powers'); it is part of the same sentence as the axe and is left without a separate citation. 'Comes unseen' renders λαθραῖον (secret, stealthy). 'The good man does good both to himself and to his neighbors' stands where Ecclesiastes 10:12a speaks of the wise man's gracious words; cited with 10:12 as one verse. No Psalm citations. 'Leap from its handle' renders ἐκπηδῆσαι and avoids the English idiom 'fly off the handle'. 'The man at this work' matches the 1622 Latin ('qui huic operi incubit').
